newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Opposition puts Australia rail sale at risk.
newsitem.headline: Opposition puts Australia rail sale at risk.

text.p: The Australian government's budget suffered a blow on Tuesday when the Labor opposition said it would vote against the planned sale of rail operator Australian National.

The other crucial minority party, the Australian Democrats, has already expressed reluctance to support the sale, which would need the approval of the upper house of parliament, the Senate, where the government does not have a majority.

"The government has given no consideration to the future employment of the hundreds, if not thousands, of workers who will be displaced by its reckless policy," Labor transport spokesman Lindsay Tanner said in a statement.

The government's May 13 budget included the sale of Australian National, a collection of loss-making federal rail operations left over after the federal and state governments merged their profitable freight services in 1993.
The value of Australian National is unknown. Analysts say budget figuring seems to value it at up to A$500 million (US$383 million).
The Democrats criticised the proposed sale two weeks ago as ill-conceived and potentially damaging for the rural economies.
They have not, however, ruled out supporting the sale if the government addressed their concerns.

The Liberal-National government is two votes short of a majority in the Senate but its first budget, which slashed A$7 billion from the deficit, survived minor-party hostility largely because two independent senators supplied those votes.
But the government last month called in the police to investigate fraud allegations against one of those independents, Mal Colston, and he is now withholding his vote.
Tanner said Labor would seek Senate deferral of the legislation, introduced into the House of Representatives this month, until the government met certain requirements.

These included a "coherent policy for the Australian rail industry" and various forms of market intervention, such as guarantees for passenger operations and funding assistance for states developing their rail infrastructure.
A spokesman for Transport Minister John Sharp said the government was still keen to sell Australian National to what he called the innovative, customer-focused private sector.
"We'll just wait and see what they (Labor) do do in the Senate," he said in response to the Opposition's announcement.
This year's budget sought to phase in government savings that would eventually be worth A$2 billion, without counting asset sales. (AS1 = US$0.765)
